issues.legal_issue: The statutory exclusion for premises belonging to a government or local authority applies to a possession suit brought by a lessee against a subtenant.
material_facts: The disputed premises were in a building erected under an arrangement with a local authority, which then leased the land and building for a long term.
The lessee’s assignee sued a monthly subtenant for possession after serving notice to quit.
The subtenant claimed the protection of the rent-control statute and objected that the civil court lacked jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion applied to the premises themselves, including in a suit between the lessee and the subtenant, so the rent-control statute did not govern the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the exclusion is framed as an immunity for premises belonging to the government or a local authority, not merely as an exemption for a landlord-and-tenant relationship with that owner. The wording contrasts with the provision’s separate exemption for relationships created by a government grant. The court held that the property-based immunity benefits a lessee deriving title from the public owner as well. It considered the purpose of protecting public property and the reasoning in Clark v. Downes and Rudler v. Franks. Section 28’s exclusive-jurisdiction rule therefore did not apply where the premises fell outside the Act.

predicates.possession_suit_by_lessee_against_subten: A lessee or a person deriving title through the lessee brings a suit against a subtenant to recover possession of the premises.
predicates.premises_belong_to_public_authority: The premises belong to the government or a local authority.

issues.definition: When a lessee or successor sues a subtenant for possession of premises belonging to a public authority, the rent-control statute does not apply to that suit.

issues.legal_issue: A building erected by a lessee under an agreement may belong to the lessor where the agreement and lease make the building part of the property demised by the lessor.
material_facts: The original arrangement required the bidder to construct a specified building on land owned by the public authority.
After construction, the authority executed a lease that demised both the land and the building for a long term.
The lease restricted the lessee’s use and alteration of the building, required its maintenance and reinstatement if damaged, and reserved inspection and re-entry rights to the lessor.
The lessee’s assignee argued that the building belonged to the lessee because the lessee’s predecessor had paid for its construction and held extensive rights of enjoyment.
issues.conclusion: The building belonged to the lessor, the local authority, and the premises therefore fell within the statutory exclusion for premises belonging to a local authority.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 105, 54 and 58 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguish a lease, which transfers a right to enjoy property, from a sale or mortgage that transfers ownership or an interest in the property. Section 108 is subject to the parties’ agreement. The court construed the building agreement and lease as making the building the lessor’s property, with the lessee receiving rights of enjoyment. It relied on Heritable Reversionary Company v. Mullar for the ordinary meaning of “property” and “belonging to.”

rule.if: public_authority_building_lease_dispute and construction_required_by_agreement and lease_demises_land_and_building and lessor_retains_control_over_building

predicates.public_authority_building_lease_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a building on public-authority land belongs to the lessor or to a lessee under a building lease.
predicates.construction_required_by_agreement: The agreement requires the lessee or the lessee’s predecessor to construct a building on the lessor’s land.
predicates.lease_demises_land_and_building: The lease grants the lessee possession or enjoyment of both the land and the completed building.
predicates.lessor_retains_control_over_building: The lease restricts the building’s use or alteration and reserves meaningful rights of oversight or control to the lessor.

issues.definition: In a public-authority building-lease dispute, a required building that is included in the demise and remains subject to the lessor’s control belongs to the lessor.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court has inherent power to decide whether it has jurisdiction over a suit, even if its inquiry leads it to conclude that it lacks jurisdiction.
material_facts: The defendant objected that the civil court lacked jurisdiction because the rent-control statute assigned the relevant matters to another court.
Resolving the objection required deciding whether the statute applied to the premises.
issues.conclusion: The civil court could determine its own jurisdiction, and the preliminary objection that it could not entertain the suit in order to decide that issue was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The court stated that a civil court has inherent jurisdiction to determine the question of its own jurisdiction, even where the result of that inquiry may be that it has no jurisdiction over the suit. No earlier case was cited for this proposition.

predicates.civil_suit_with_jurisdiction_objection: A party to a civil suit objects that the court lacks jurisdiction to hear it.

issues.definition: When a party objects to jurisdiction in a civil suit, the court may decide whether it has jurisdiction.
